title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words
summary: Clarifies that the key words in RFC 2119 only have their special meaning when written in uppercase. Lowercase uses are ordinary English. It updates RFC 2119 and is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Shouting words like MUST means the rule is serious. If it is whispered in lowercase, it is just a normal word.

subtitle: A short fix that says only ALL-CAPS MUST and SHOULD carry the special RFC 2119 meanings.

tldr.problem: RFC 2119 said its key words are 'often capitalized', which left readers unsure how to treat lowercase 'must' and 'should'.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8174 replaces one paragraph of RFC 2119 so that the key words have their defined meanings only when written in all capitals; otherwise they are ordinary English.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2119 and supplies a new boilerplate sentence that cites BCP 14 and tests for all capitals.

today: RFC 8174 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2119; it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Ambiguity
sections.content:
RFC 2119 defines common key words such as MUST, SHOULD and MAY for protocol specifications. It says they 'are often capitalized', and that wording caused confusion about how to read lowercase 'must' and 'should'.

RFC 8174 updates RFC 2119 to settle this. It is part of BCP 14.
sections.plainLanguage: A rulebook said special words were 'often' in capitals. People did not know if small-letter versions counted too.

sections.title: What Changes in RFC 2119
sections.content:
The RFC swaps an OLD paragraph of RFC 2119 for a NEW one. Three points in the new text matter:

  • The words can be used as defined, but using them is not required. Normative text does not need the key words, and a lot of normative text does not use them and is still normative.
  • The words have the specified meanings only when they are in all capitals.
  • When not capitalized, they have their normal English meanings and are not affected by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Capital MUST is a stop sign with a legal meaning. Small 'must' is just a word in a sentence.

sections.title: The Updated Boilerplate
sections.content: Authors who follow the guidelines should place a phrase near the start of their document. The new phrase adds NOT RECOMMENDED to the list of key words and says they are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 'when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here'.
sections.plainLanguage: Documents add a sentence that says: the big-letter words are the special ones, and only those.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content: The document needs no IANA actions. It calls itself purely procedural and says there are no related security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: It only changes how a rule is written down, so it creates no new danger.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
